q: Explain the Gargano classification of rum, and why rum needed one.
accept: pure single rum single blended traditional and modern classified by still type
gargano classifies by distillation method because rum has no global legal framework
pot still from one distillery is pure single rum column is traditional modern is multi-column
a method-based classification answering undeclared additives and meaningless age claims
ans: Luca Gargano, with Richard Seale, proposed classifying rum by how it is distilled rather than by colour, age claim or country. Pure Single Rum: 100% pot still, from one distillery. Single Blended Rum: pot and traditional column blended, still from one distillery. Traditional Rum: traditional column still. Modern or Industrial Rum: multi-column, high-purity spirit. It exists because rum has no global rulebook — minimum ages differ island by island, 'solera' and a big number on the label can mean almost anything, tropical ageing consumes spirit several times faster than continental, and many producers add sugar, glycerol and colouring after distillation with no obligation to declare it. Method is the one axis a buyer can verify.
exp: Two follow-ups always come. First, 'single' means one distillery, exactly as in Scotch — never one barrel. Second, tropical versus continental ageing is why a twelve-year Caribbean rum can show more maturity than a twenty-year Scotch, and why the same distillate bottled in Europe tastes younger. For a list, the practical move is to buy by still type and by disclosed additives.

q: Explain the louche in absinthe, and settle the thujone question.
accept: anethole is soluble in alcohol but not water so it emulsifies and clouds the drink
the louche is anise oil coming out of solution and thujone is not a hallucinogen
oils emulsify on dilution and the eu caps thujone at 35 mg per kilo
anise oil precipitates as an emulsion and the absinthe madness story is a myth
ans: The louche is an emulsion. Anise oils — anethole from green anise and star anise, along with fenchone — dissolve readily in high-strength ethanol but not in water. Add iced water and they come out of solution as microscopic droplets that scatter light, so the drink turns opalescent and the aroma is released. A slow, thick louche is fair evidence of a distilled, herb-forward absinthe rather than a dyed and flavoured spirit, though it can be faked by adding oils post-distillation. Thujone comes from grande wormwood, Artemisia absinthium. It is not a hallucinogen; at the concentrations present it is a mild GABA-receptor antagonist. The EU caps it at 35 mg/kg and the US requires effectively thujone-free spirit at under 10 ppm — and when surviving pre-ban bottles were analysed, they sat within those modern limits. The nineteenth-century madness was cheap adulterants, spirit at 70% abv, and a temperance movement that needed a villain at exactly the moment the post-phylloxera wine lobby wanted its shelf space back.
exp: The service ritual follows directly from the chemistry: three to five parts iced water added slowly, sugar only if the absinthe is bitter enough to need it. If a bottle refuses to louche, it was probably never distilled with anise in the first place.

q: What makes a wine legally a vermouth, and how should a wine-led bar treat it?
accept: an aromatised wine at least 75 percent wine flavoured with artemisia
wine based at 14.5 to 22 percent abv with wormwood and it must be refrigerated once open
minimum 75% wine plus species of artemisia treat it as wine rather than as a spirit
fortified aromatised wine with wormwood that oxidises and needs cold storage
ans: Under the EU's aromatised wine product rules, vermouth is an aromatised wine: at least 75% wine by volume, fortified to between 14.5% and 22% abv, and flavoured principally with species of Artemisia — wormwood is the non-negotiable botanical, and the name itself comes from the German Wermut. Sweetening is permitted, colour usually arrives as caramel, and the styles run dry, blanc or bianco, rosso and rosé, with Vermouth di Torino and Chambéry carrying geographical protection. The service lesson follows from the legal definition: it is wine, so it oxidises like wine. Refrigerate it once opened, date the bottle, pour it out inside two to four weeks, and buy in small format if volume is low. A stale bottle of vermouth ruins more Martinis and Manhattans than any other single failure behind a bar.
exp: The trap is calling vermouth a spirit and storing it accordingly. It is wine, it dies like wine, and a bar keeping it at room temperature is serving oxidised wine in every stirred drink it makes. Turin's sweet rosso tradition and the drier Marseille and Chambéry style are the two poles worth stocking.

q: Explain the sour template, and how the schools of ratio differ.
accept: spirit citrus sweetener with 2:1:1 as the standard embury at 8:2:1 and equal parts
a sour is strong sour sweet and the schools run from two one one to equal parts
two parts spirit one citrus one sweet with the equal parts family as the other pole
the template is base citrus sugar and embury preferred a much drier eight two one
ans: Every sour is the same three parts — base spirit, citrus, sweetener — and the canon is variations on their proportions. The modern bar standard is 2:1:1: two parts spirit, one part citrus, one part simple syrup. That is the Daiquiri exactly, the Whiskey Sour, and the Margarita once orange liqueur takes the sweetener's place. David Embury argued for 8:2:1, far drier and far more spirit-forward, writing for palates shaped by richer pre-war ingredients. The equal-parts school — the Last Word, Corpse Reviver No. 2, Paper Plane, and the Negroni on the aromatic side — only works when the modifiers are themselves complex and bittersweet enough to justify occupying a quarter of the glass each. From there the moves are: egg white for texture, a bitter or amaro for length, splitting the base, swapping syrup for a liqueur. What you actually adjust night to night is the fruit's sugar and acidity on the day.
exp: Answer with a template and one worked example rather than a list of recipes — that is what separates a master candidate from a well-read enthusiast. It is also a working tool on the floor: any unfamiliar drink can be reverse-engineered as a sour, an aromatic (spirit, sugar, bitters), or a highball, and built from first principles when the recipe is unavailable.
